body_markdown:
This year’s Ignite was all about shoring up trust and reliability. Unlike last year, which focused heavily on a fictious frontier company for examples, Microsoft brought to the stage Accenture, Alaska Airlines, Blackrock, BNY, Chevron, Publicis Europe, Unilever, and others. These companies lent real-world credence to the idea that Microsoft remains a trusted enterprise partner in an agentic world.


However, for the second time in three weeks, Microsoft also had to begin a keynote by talking about what it needs to fix (the last time was GitHub Universe). This was necessary considering the outage from the previous week and the large number of enterprise IT attendees at the event that are increasingly worrying about reliability.


After the mea culpa, it was time to turn to new announcements, with the stars naturally being AI & data.


#### AI Transparency And Cost Reduction Efforts Took Center Stage


Most of the conference was about transparency and resiliency in the agentic age. The AI Transparency Initiative, created with 40 other companies, primarily focuses on Microsoft’s own models but also addresses competing models. Observability was also brought up in the form of tools like Agent 365. Both of these are welcome efforts in a world where visibility into what AI agents are doing (and the permissions they’re doing it with) are facing increasing scrutiny.


Microsoft also spent a lot of time on model cost, latency, and routing. This focused on their own MAI models and specialized security models such as MAI Cyber. In some ways, Microsoft is lining themselves up for a post-frontier model world when models become commoditized. They emphasized that you don’t need to spend cash on frontier models when a faster, cheaper model can produce desired outcomes.


#### Microsoft IQ Addresses The Growing Context Layer


Following last year’s introduction of key data capabilities, this year focused on connecting the data dots. The company focused heavily on Microsoft IQ, a combination of Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, and Web IQ. Work IQ, in particular, is storing a staggering 20 exabytes of data for M365 customers today.


While some elements of Microsoft IQ were perplexing (customers we talked to said they were confused as to if they needed to purchase all four products) the capabilities added, such as Fabric Apps, should breathe more life into creating business intelligence software.


#### Agentic Security is Bigger Than the SOC


Microsoft’s security announcements indicate that silos will be disrupted and organizational structures will need to change. Growing vulnerability volume and easier access to AI models and pentesting frameworks, like Artex, are changing what Microsoft calls the “physics of cyber.” Its answer is Perception, which combines security signals, controls, context, models, and harnesses to power red, blue, and green agents. As these agents coordinate work, the boundaries between the SOC, exposure management, offensive security, IT, identity, and application security are increasingly blurred.


However, don’t confused agentic with autonomous. In Perception, playbooks coordinate around outcomes across Microsoft’s security stack and security team members must design those playbooks. Context is also in the control plane, at least when it comes to security. Microsoft showed agents combining attack paths, asset criticality, threat intelligence, identity, endpoint, and vulnerability data. We agree with this direction. In the end, the differentiator will increasingly be the ability to assemble trustworthy security context, connect it to controls, and use it to improve posture or respond to threats regardless of which model sits underneath.


#### Azure Focuses On AI Sustainability


Cloud was woven throughout Microsoft’s presentations, but the biggest applause at the keynote was for Microsoft’s “community-first” approach to AI infrastructure. It’s built on five tenants:


- “Paying their way” to make sure electricity prices don’t increase dramatically in communities near Azure data centers


- Minimizing the use of and replenishing water


- Creating jobs


- Adding to the tax base funding local hospital, schools, and public facilities


- Investing in local AI training


While some of these are more aspirational (in most communities, data consistently shows electricity prices increase, not decrease, when data centers are built nearby) the recognition that this is an industry-wide challenge was appreciated with the customers Forrester spoke to.


#### Trying To Make Copilot The Hub For Multiplayer AI


The last major focus area of Microsoft is Copilot. After throwing shade at Anthropic and OpenAI for their collaboration efforts, Microsoft focused on the functional pieces it’s delivering for different business functions (e.g., sales, legal, finance, etc.). They also announced a needed (and, quite frankly, overdue) partnership with SalesForce for Copilot.


However, the biggest area of improvement was in multiplayer AI. Microsoft wants Copilot to be the central hub for teams to collaborate. In particular, they want multiple users engaging AI in complex workflows at the same time through Copilot, otherwise known as multiplayer AI. Multiplayer AI is a relatively new concept, so this will take time to bear fruit, but it’s where the future is going for collaboration.


#### The “Frontier” Becomes More Real


In recent years, Microsoft has focused on “frontier organizations” – enterprises that take advantage of AI to completely remake their businesses. While most customers we talked to are looking at the frontier as aspirational and not currently achievable, there were signs at this year’s Ignite that they were taking Microsoft’s message more seriously. Right now, though, we need to focus on the basics: Keeping systems resilient and secure and in an increasingly agentic world.
